xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoA currency dealer at a bank in Seoul, South Korea, November 6, 2026 [Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters]By John PowerPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026Asian stock markets have slumped as concerns that the AI boom is losing steam dog major players in tech.

Markets in South Korea and Hong Kong sank deeper into the red on Monday, continuing Friday’s tech-led sell-off on both sides of the Pacific – though US tech stocks looked set to bounce back upon the resumption of trading on Wall Street.

The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi) in Seoul slid as much as 5.8 percent, before closing down 3.3 percent.

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, major players in the AI race as the world’s top two memory chip makers, fell 3.1 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped 0.1 percent, after an earlier decline of nearly 2 percent.

The CSI 300 Index in Shanghai edged up 0.1 percent, reversing an earlier decline of more than 1 percent.

After opening lower, the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (Taiex) in Taipei closed up 2.2 percent.

Japan’s stock markets were closed for Labour Thanksgiving Day.

Following Friday’s rout in Asia, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 closed 3.7 percent lower to enter a correction – the term investors use when the market drops 10 percent or more from its recent high.

The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite, roughly half of which is made up of the “Magnificent Seven” AI-oriented firms, dropped 5.3 percent to erase all of its gains for 2026.

The Kospi, Nikkei 225, and the Taiex all entered the weekend deep in the red, closing between 5.1 percent and 6.2 percent lower.

The Hang Seng Index finished Friday down 1.9 percent.

Wall Street was headed for a strong rebound on Monday, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures up 2.2 percent and 2.9 percent, respectively.

After last week’s losses, investors are trying to assess if the market correction has “gone too far”, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale.

“I think markets are trying to find some ground after a massive sell-off in [the] US on Friday, a more than a three-standard-deviation event in tech indices,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera.

Investors have long been concerned that tech firms may not be able to sustain the multi-trillion-dollar investments they have poured into the infrastructure needed to train and run AI.

Global AI-related investment is expected to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

The debt-fuelled investment splurge has stirred intense debate about whether tech firms are creating a stock market bubble similar to the one that emerged in the run-up to the dot-com crash in 2000.

Concerns that the AI boom may be coming to an end have been exacerbated by growing calls for greater oversight of the sector.

The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the US midterm elections is expected to slow data centre construction in US states, while the alleged espionage scandal embroiling chip giant Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has led to a push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips.

“AI-related concerns will continue to dominate this week, as investors try to determine if the bottom is near,” Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, told Al Jazeera.

“A bright spot is that US equity futures are up and South Korea reported very strong exports for the first 20 days of November, driven by semiconductor exports, which are up 294.4 percent year-on-year,” Goh said.
